objectives: Explain Layered security and enterprise architecture in beginner-friendly language and then use the correct professional terminology.
Perform a controlled practical task related to Layered security and enterprise architecture and produce reproducible evidence.

lesson.prerequisites: Review the preceding topic in Security architecture and Zero Trust and complete the academy lab safety briefing. No external target is permitted.

blocks.title: Detailed teaching notes
blocks.body:
Layered security and enterprise architecture is taught as a professional capability inside security engineering, cloud, containers and secure software. Start with the simplest mental model: identify the system or process, identify what normal behaviour looks like, then observe what changes when a controlled action is performed. In Security architecture and Zero Trust, the learner should be able to explain the idea in plain language before using specialist terminology. The important question is not only ‘what is this?’ but also ‘why does it exist, how does it behave, what evidence does it produce, and when would a professional choose it?’ Work from observable evidence such as command output, configuration values, logs, packet captures, application responses, alerts or documented decisions. Never substitute assumptions for evidence. When a task could affect another system, use only the named Marian laboratory and follow its scope. Build a habit of recording the starting state, the action taken, the result, and the recovery or rollback path. This makes your work reproducible and makes later troubleshooting much faster. Finally, connect the technique to a security outcome: confidentiality, integrity, availability, identity assurance, detection, response, resilience, risk reduction or safe delivery.

Detailed notes: Before making a change, define the expected result and one observation that would prove it. During the task, change one meaningful variable at a time so cause and effect remain clear. After the task, compare the observed result with the expected result and record discrepancies rather than hiding them. If the result is unexpected, classify the problem as a configuration issue, dependency issue, permission issue, data issue, timing issue or tool limitation before changing anything else. Professional practice also includes least privilege, safe handling of credentials, careful evidence preservation, and clear escalation when the evidence is insufficient.

Professional depth: In real work, the same technical fact can have different meanings depending on asset criticality, identity, network location, business function and time. Learn to ask what asset is affected, who owns it, what normal looks like, what changed, how confident the evidence is, and what action has the lowest safe blast radius. A strong practitioner can also communicate the finding to three audiences: another technical practitioner who needs reproducibility, a manager who needs impact and priority, and an affected user who needs a clear next step. This communication skill is part of cybersecurity competence because correct technical work that cannot be explained or safely operationalized is difficult to defend, audit or maintain.

blocks.title: Three-part practical: guided → investigation → challenge
instructions: Guided task: Open the authorized virtual-enterprise environment, read the scope banner, verify the supplied target and record the starting state. Perform the documented Layered security and enterprise architecture task one step at a time. Capture the key output or screenshot after each meaningful milestone.

Investigation task: Change one safe variable, repeat the observation and compare the two results. Explain what changed, why it changed and which evidence supports your conclusion. If the result differs from expectation, troubleshoot using evidence before trying a new change.

Independent challenge: Repeat the objective without following the exact guided sequence. Produce a short professional note containing objective, scope, method, evidence, result, limitation and recommended next action.

Evidence task: Save only the evidence needed to prove competence. Label files with a timestamp, task identifier and short description. Do not store passwords, API keys or other secrets in the evidence workspace.
Reset task: Restore the lab to its clean state and confirm the environment is ready for another learner.

blocks.title: Three-part practical: guided → investigation → challenge
instructions: Guided task: Open the authorized container-k8s environment, read the scope banner, verify the supplied target and record the starting state. Perform the documented DevSecOps pipelines and security automation task one step at a time. Capture the key output or screenshot after each meaningful milestone.

Investigation task: Change one safe variable, repeat the observation and compare the two results. Explain what changed, why it changed and which evidence supports your conclusion. If the result differs from expectation, troubleshoot using evidence before trying a new change.

Independent challenge: Repeat the objective without following the exact guided sequence. Produce a short professional note containing objective, scope, method, evidence, result, limitation and recommended next action.

Evidence task: Save only the evidence needed to prove competence. Label files with a timestamp, task identifier and short description. Do not store passwords, API keys or other secrets in the evidence workspace.
Reset task: Restore the lab to its clean state and confirm the environment is ready for another learner.
success_checks: Scope and authorization are confirmed before technical interaction.
The learner can reproduce the expected result and explain the mechanism behind it.
Evidence is sufficient for another practitioner to verify the conclusion.
The learner identifies at least one limitation, failure mode or alternative explanation.
The lab is returned to a clean state without affecting external systems.
hints: Start by checking what is already true before changing anything.
Use one variable at a time.
When a result is surprising, preserve the evidence before retrying.

success_checks: The objective is measurable.

blocks.title: Scenario-based professional decision
blocks.question: You are working on an authorized academy exercise involving DevSecOps pipelines and security automation. The first result is ambiguous and could have more than one explanation. What should you do next?

items.prompt: Which approach best demonstrates professional understanding of DevSecOps pipelines and security automation?

choices.text: Memorize terminology without testing behaviour
Observe normal behaviour, perform a controlled task, and explain the evidence
Change many variables at once
Skip documentation if the tool reports success

items.prompt: What should you do when the observed result differs from the expected result?

choices.text: Delete the evidence and start again
Preserve the evidence, compare assumptions, and troubleshoot systematically
Assume the tool is wrong
Move immediately to a different target

items.prompt: Where should a potentially disruptive security technique be practised?

choices.text: A public system found during research
A production system without approval
An explicitly authorized isolated academy laboratory
Any internet-connected device

items.prompt: What makes evidence useful to another practitioner?

choices.text: It contains as much raw output as possible
It is labelled, relevant, reproducible and tied to a conclusion
It contains credentials so the reviewer can log in
It omits failed attempts

items.prompt: What is the best final question after completing a practical task?

choices.text: Can I make the system behave differently?
What security or operational outcome does this capability support, and what limitation remains?
How quickly can I repeat the command?
Can I skip the reset?

lesson.revision_notes: Revision guide: explain DevSecOps pipelines and security automation without jargon first, then define the professional terms. Review the baseline → action → evidence → interpretation → decision workflow. Re-run the guided practical from a clean state, then complete the independent challenge. Before moving on, make sure you can explain one common failure mode, one security implication, and one safe recovery path. Build a compact personal cheat sheet containing commands, concepts, diagrams or decision rules that you genuinely understand rather than copying a list without context.

NIST NICE Framework Components v2.2.0 for professional work-role and competency language.
Official documentation for the operating system, protocol, security product or cloud service used in this lesson.
OWASP guidance where the lesson concerns application or API security.
evidence_requirements: short explanation of what the evidence proves
professional_notes: Never place credentials or secrets in learner evidence.
Prefer reproducible observations over screenshots without context.
When unsure, stop, preserve evidence and escalate rather than broadening scope.
Treat failed attempts as useful diagnostic information when documented clearly.
